1a.html:
Recycling as a source of metals

Metals extracted from ores are primary; metals recovered from scrap are secondary. Scrap is now a major source of metals because:

  1. It is already metallic: it needs only refining, and in the best cases only melting. In primary extraction most of the energy goes into breaking metal-oxygen or metal-sulphur bonds; scrap skips that step, and also mining and ore dressing.
  2. Energy saving: about 95% for Al, 85% for Cu, 60-75% for steel and 65% for Pb.
  3. Less pollution: fewer and simpler operations; CO2 falls by about 90% (Al), 65% (Cu) and 50% (steel), against primary metallurgy's 7-9% share of world CO2. No mine, no tailings.
  4. Conservation of resources: high-grade deposits are limited. Copper deposits worked a century ago held about 4% Cu; new mines treat 1% Cu or less, so primary metal costs ever more energy.
  5. Large supply, same quality: in 2003 the US recycled nearly 13 million vehicles (over 14 Mt of steel scrap), and Bangladesh's steel scrap is mostly from ship-breaking. Secondary metal cannot be told from primary by any test.

Classification of scrap by availability

  1. Home scrap: generated during the production of primary or secondary metal (defective castings, croppings, sheet edge trimmings). It needs no collection or sorting and is always recycled.
  2. Prompt industrial scrap: generated in manufacturing metal articles (turnings, punchings, offcuts); welded structures give little, machined parts up to 50%. Recycled within a short time, whatever the scrap price.
  3. Obsolete scrap: from products no longer useful (old railway lines, machinery, automobiles, ships). Supply depends on product lifetime (car 10-12 years, lead-acid battery 2-4 years) and on scrap price; it is mixed and must be collected and sorted, a labour-intensive step.
pts: Scrap is already metallic, so only refining or melting are needed; bond-breaking reduction, mining and dressing are saved
Energy savings with numbers: about 95% Al, 85% Cu, 60-75% steel (or 65% Pb)
Less pollution with a number (CO2 cut about 90% Al, 65% Cu, 50% steel, or primary metal 7-9% of world CO2) and no mine or tailings
Conservation of limited high-grade ore: Cu grade fell from about 4% to 1% or less
Size of the supply (US vehicles, Bangladesh ship scrap) or equal quality of secondary metal
Home scrap: defined as scrap from metal production, with an example, always recycled
Prompt industrial scrap: defined as scrap from manufacturing, with an example, recycled quickly whatever the price

1b.html:
The oceans hold metals in two forms.

  1. Sea water covers nearly 70% of the earth's surface and is a dilute solution of about 3.5% dissolved solids with about 70 elements. Na (10,500 g per tonne) and Mg (1270 g per tonne) are abundant; a cubic kilometre of sea water holds about 1.3 million tonnes of Mg, and magnesium and salt are produced commercially from it. Cu, Zn and Au (0.000005 g per tonne) are too dilute to recover.
  2. Manganese nodules cover the deep-sea floor: about 1.5 trillion tonnes in the Pacific alone, averaging about 24% Mn and 14% Fe with Ni, Cu and Co. They hold about 358 billion tonnes of Mn, 14.7 billion of Ni and 5.2 billion of Co, far more than land reserves. They are also renewable: about 10 million tonnes form each year, while land deposits are being depleted.

Limitation: the nodules lie at about 5000 m, so collection is costly and environmentally sensitive; they are mainly a future reserve.
pts: Sea water: about 70% of the surface, about 3.5% dissolved solids, about 70 elements, a huge dilute solution

Limitation: depth about 5000 m, costly collection and environmental concern

1c.html:
Why drying is expensive

Drying removes water by converting it to vapour, which a gas current carries away. Heat must raise the water to its boiling point and then supply the latent heat of evaporation (2257 kJ/kg at 100 C); water's specific heat and latent heat are both large, about 2.57 MJ per kg of water from 25 C, all from fuel. Heat is also lost with the hot exhaust gas and in heating the solids, and the gas raises dust. Thickening (40-50 % water left) and filtration (about 10 %) remove water as a liquid with little energy, so drying is the most expensive step and is used only for the last water, when later steps need a dry product.

Drying in a rotary cylindrical dryer

  1. A sheet-steel cylinder, 5-30 m long and 0.9-3.0 m in diameter, sloping 3-5 degrees, rests on rollers and turns at 1.5-2 rpm.
  2. Wet material is fed continuously at the raised end.
  3. Lifting flights turn the material over and over through the gas and stop it sticking; the slope moves it toward the discharge end.
  4. Hot combustion gases (750-1000 C) enter at the discharge end and flow counter-current, so the hottest, driest gas removes the last traces of moisture efficiently; the moist gas leaves at the feed end.
  5. Dry solids discharge continuously at the lower end.
pts: Drying converts water to vapour, needing sensible heat and the large latent heat of evaporation (about 2260 kJ/kg)
The heat comes from fuel, with extra losses (exhaust gas, heating the solids, dust)
Contrast: thickening and filtration remove liquid water mechanically and cheaply, so drying is used only for the last water
Construction: steel cylinder 5-30 m long, 0.9-3.0 m diameter, slope 3-5 degrees, 1.5-2 rpm
Fed at the raised end; flights turn the material over through the gas and move it to the discharge end
Hot gases (750-1000 C) flow counter-current, so the hottest, driest gas removes the last traces of moisture; moist gas leaves at the feed end

2a.html:
A smooth roll crusher breaks particles by compression alone, and only those it can nip: with roll radius R, gap d and particle radius r,

\cos\alpha = \frac{R + d/2}{R + r},\qquad \text{nipped if } \tan\alpha \le \mu

with an angle of nip 2\alpha of about 32°. So 1 m rolls set 12.5 mm apart take lumps of only about 53 mm, a reduction ratio near 4.

Advantages of toothed (corrugated or breaker-bar) rolls:

  1. No nip limit: the teeth grip and draw in the lumps, so they reduce much larger particles for a given roll size (heavy double-roll crushers take feed up to about 500 mm).
  2. Compression, impact and shear, not compression alone: the teeth literally tear the particles apart.
  3. Hence suited to weak, ductile or soft materials such as coal, which smooth rolls would only squeeze.
  4. More versatile: one toothed roll can work against a stationary curved breaker plate.

Limitation: they cannot handle very hard solids; smooth rolls give few fines and virtually no oversize.
pts: Smooth rolls act by compression only and are limited by nip (\cos\alpha = (R + d/2)/(R + r), angle of nip about 32°), so the feed is only a few times the gap (about 4 for 1 m rolls set 12.5 mm apart)
Toothed rolls are not limited by nip and can reduce much larger particles (feed up to about 500 mm)
Toothed rolls break by compression, impact and shear; the teeth tear the particles apart
Suited to weak, ductile or soft materials such as coal
More versatile (single roll against a breaker plate), with the limitation that very hard solids cannot be handled

A jaw crusher breaks every lump by compression (slide 9 says so itself): the swing jaw moves slowly and least near the pivot at the top, so the large lumps there are nipped and squeezed, not struck.
2b.html:
Working (Blake jaw crusher). Feed enters between two jaws set in a V open at the top. The fixed (anvil) jaw is nearly vertical; the swing jaw, pivoted at the top, makes 20 to 30° with it. An eccentric on the flywheel shaft drives a pitman up and down, which straightens and bends two toggle plates (one pinned to the frame, one to the swing jaw) and so moves the bottom of the swing jaw towards the fixed jaw and back, 250 to 400 times per minute. Lumps caught between the upper parts of the jaws are broken by compression, drop into the narrower space below and are re-crushed at the next closing, until they pass the throat. Most discharge occurs while the jaw recedes. Flywheels even out this intermittent load.

Important characteristics.

  1. Size: quoted as gape × jaw width; a 66 × 84 in crusher takes rock under 66 in.
  2. Set and stroke: the set (average, often minimum, throat opening) fixes the product size; the stroke (throw) is the difference between the open and closed throat openings, short for brittle rock (quartz) and long for tough rock that deforms.
  3. Reduction ratio = gape / set; the actual value is lower, since the largest feed lumps are smaller than the gape.
  4. Capacity and power: capacity (t/h of product) rises with speed and falls as the reduction ratio rises; power is proportional to the crushing done, and power per tonne is higher in small crushers.
  5. Blake against Dodge: the Blake jaw moves most at the bottom of the V, so it hardly chokes; the Dodge crusher (pivot at the bottom) gives little oversize but many fines, and tends to choke.
  6. Wear: cast steel jaws with manganese steel liners; wear enlarges the set, so it must be adjusted often.
pts: Construction: nearly vertical fixed jaw and a swing jaw pivoted at the top, forming a V at 20 to 30°
Drive: eccentric, pitman and toggles move the bottom of the swing jaw 250 to 400 times per minute; flywheels even out the intermittent load
Action: lumps nipped and broken by compression near the top, fall into the narrower space and are re-crushed until they pass the throat
Size quoted as gape × width (66 × 84 in), the gape fixing the largest lump accepted
Set (throat opening, fixes product size) and stroke or throw (short for brittle, long for tough rock) defined
Reduction ratio = gape / set, the actual value lower than calculated
Capacity rises with speed and falls with reduction ratio; power per tonne higher in small crushers
Blake (pivot at top, greatest motion at the bottom, no choking) contrasted with Dodge (pivot at bottom, little oversize but many fines, chokes)
Manganese steel liners whose wear enlarges the set, so the set must be adjusted

"Crushing mills" here means crushing machines (crushers); revolving mills are the tumbling rod, ball and autogenous mills.

BasisCrushing machinesRevolving (tumbling) mills
Feed and product sizethe gape limits the feed and the set fixes the largest productopenings at both ends are much larger than the particles, so little restriction on feed or product size
Sizingbuilt into the machine (the set)none inherent; closed circuit with a classifier gives a closely sized product
How energy is applieddirectly to the ore particles by the moving partinto rotating the mill and its charge; breakage follows from the motion of the charge
Crushing elementsfixed relative to one another, so the set must be adjusted as the faces wearfree media (rods, balls, ore) held apart only by the ore, so no set adjustment
Productcoarse, down to about 6 mmfine, below 6 mm to micrometres
Actionmainly compression, preferentially on the largest piecesimpact and abrasion, less selective, so fines are over-ground
Operationusually dry, free discharge through the throatbatch or continuous, often wet; peripheral or trunnion discharge through a grate
Examplesjaw, gyratory, cone and roll crushersrod, ball and autogenous mills

Consequences. Because a mill keeps grinding particles that are already fine, ball mills are run in closed circuit with a classifier, whereas a crusher's set already limits its product. Wet grinding in mills wears the media faster but saves energy and eases classification. The stamp mill lies between the two classes.
pts: Size restriction: in crushers the gape and set limit feed and product size, while mills, with large end openings, impose little restriction and have no inherent sizing
Energy: applied directly to the particles in crushers, but used to rotate the mill and charge in mills, breakage resulting from the charge motion

Product size: coarse (to about 6 mm) from crushers, fine (below 6 mm) from mills

Consequence: mills need closed circuit with a classifier; or operation differs (dry free discharge against wet, batch or continuous, trunnion or peripheral discharge)

3a.html:
Recovery is the percentage of the total metal contained in the ore (feed) that is recovered in the concentrate. A recovery of 90% means 90% of the metal reports to the concentrate and 10% is lost in the tailing. It shows how the metal of the heads is distributed among the products.

Ratio of concentration is the weight of feed (heads) treated to obtain one unit weight of concentrate: 1 t of concentrate from 20 t of ore is a ratio of 20 to 1.

The two are essentially independent, so both are needed to judge an operation: picking a few lumps of pure galena from a ton of lead ore gives a high grade and ratio but a very low recovery.

Derivation (two-product formula).

Step 1, notation. Feed of weight F and assay f gives a concentrate C, c and a tailing T, t (assays as metal fractions). By definition

R = \frac{Cc}{Ff}\times 100, \qquad K = \frac{F}{C}

Step 2, weight balance. All the feed leaves as concentrate or tailing:

F = C + T \qquad (1)

Step 3, metal balance. With strictly correct sampling, weighing and assaying:

Ff = Cc + Tt \qquad (2)

Step 4, eliminate T. Multiply (1) by t, Ft = Ct + Tt (3), and subtract (3) from (2):

F(f - t) = C(c - t) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{F}{C} = \frac{c - t}{f - t}

Step 5, ratio of concentration:

K = \frac{c - t}{f - t}

Step 6, recovery. Substitute C/F = (f - t)/(c - t) into the definition:

\boxed{R = \frac{c\,(f - t)}{f\,(c - t)} \times 100}

Use. Only the assays are needed, which helps when weights are not available. For a lead flotation test with f = 2.1\%, c = 55.1\%, t = 0.1\% Pb:

K = \frac{0.551 - 0.001}{0.021 - 0.001} = 27.5, \qquad R = \frac{0.551 \times 0.020}{0.021 \times 0.550}\times 100 = 95.4\%

so 4.6% of the lead is lost in the tailing. The same formula serves a classifier, with f, c, t the percentages of a size fraction in feed, overflow and sand.
pts: Defines recovery as the percentage of the metal in the feed that reports to the concentrate, R = Cc/Ff \times 100 (90% example)
Defines ratio of concentration as weight of feed per unit weight of concentrate, F/C (for example 20 to 1)
Notes that recovery and ratio are independent and both are needed (galena hand-picking example)
Sets out the notation F, C, T and f, c, t (or the flowsheet)
Weight balance F = C + T
Metal balance Ff = Cc + Tt, assuming correct sampling, weighing and assaying
Multiplies the weight balance by t and subtracts to get F(f - t) = C(c - t)
Ratio of concentration F/C = (c - t)/(f - t)
Recovery R = c(f - t)/[f(c - t)] \times 100, boxed
Notes that only assays are needed, or checks the result with a numerical example (27.5 to 1, 95.4%)

3b.html:
A particle smaller than the aperture does not pass at once, for two reasons.

1. Probability of hitting the screen matrix. Only part of the screen area is open, so a particle may land on the wire. For a sphere of diameter d on a square aperture D_A with wire D_W:

P = \left(\frac{D_A - d}{D_A + D_W}\right)^2

With D_W = D_A and d = 0.5D_A, P \approx 6\%, so about 36 presentations are needed for a 90% chance. Particles must be presented to the screen many times.

2. Blinding. Particles just greater than the aperture wedge in the openings and block them.

Role of the two movements.

  • Vertical movement lifts particles out of the blocking positions (unblinds the apertures) and loosens the bed so fines work down to the deck.
  • Horizontal movement ensures that, when the particles fall back under gravity, they land at different positions on the screen, and carries the oversize along so fresh feed reaches the deck.

Vertical motion alone drops a particle back on the same spot; sliding alone leaves blinding particles wedged. The vibrating screen gives both and is much more efficient than a static bar screen.
pts: Only part of the screen is open: a particle may hit the matrix, so it must be presented many times (probability of passage, for example [(D_A - d)/(D_A + D_W)]^2)
Near-mesh particles blind the apertures
Vertical movement lifts blinding particles out of the apertures and loosens the bed
Horizontal movement presents the falling particles at different positions and conveys the oversize
Either movement alone fails (same aperture again, or blinding particles stay wedged)
Vibrating screen provides both and is far more efficient than a static bar screen

3c.html:
Classification is a method of separating mineral particles of various sizes, shapes and specific gravities into two or more products on the basis of the velocity with which they fall through a fluid (usually water: wet classifying). Coarse, heavier and rounder grains settle faster than finer, lighter and more angular ones. It is used for particles too fine to be screened efficiently.

Principle.

  1. Terminal velocity. Gravity (less buoyancy) accelerates a particle, while the fluid resistance rises with velocity. When they balance, the particle reaches its terminal velocity and falls uniformly.
  2. Resistance. At low velocity it is viscous (shear); at high velocity turbulent (fluid displacement). In the viscous range Stokes' law applies:
v_t = \frac{d^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)\,g}{18\,\mu}

For equal density the larger particle falls faster; for equal size the denser one does.

  1. Sorting column. Fluid rises at a uniform velocity V: particles with v_t > V sink to the spigot, those with v_t < V go to the overflow.
  2. Size and density together. In water, 50 μm galena (7.5) settles with quartz (2.7) of about 98 μm.
  3. Free and hindered settling. Below about 15% solids particles settle freely and size dominates; in denser pulps the pulp acts as a heavy liquid and density gains weight.
pts: Defines classification: separation into two or more products by settling velocity in a fluid, which depends on size, specific gravity and shape
Coarse, heavy, round grains settle faster; used for particles too fine to screen
Gravity against resistance rising with velocity; at balance, terminal velocity and uniform fall
Viscous and turbulent resistance; Stokes' law or the rule that larger or denser particles settle faster
Sorting column (described or sketched): fluid rising at V; v_t > V to the spigot, v_t < V to the overflow
Size and density act together, for example equal-settling 50 μm galena and about 98 μm quartz
Free settling below about 15% solids (size dominant) against hindered settling in denser pulps (pulp acts as a heavy liquid, density gains weight)

4a.html:
Principle. A magnetic separator gives a magnetic path and a gravitational path: magnetic particles stay in the field, the others pass through. The pull on a particle of volume V and susceptibility \chi is

F = \frac{\chi V}{\mu_0}\,B\frac{dB}{dx}

so weakly magnetic minerals need a strong field with a steep gradient. In the disc separator the field is raised in stages, so minerals of progressively weaker susceptibility are taken off one after another.

Construction.

  • A horizontal conveyor belt (or vibrating tray) carries the dry feed in a thin layer, about one particle deep.
  • Electromagnet poles sit under the belt.
  • Above the belt, two or three discs on vertical shafts rotate in a horizontal plane. Each disc is magnetised by the magnet below and acts as the opposite pole; its sharp-edged rim concentrates the flux, giving the high gradient.
  • Each disc overhangs the edge of the belt, with a side chute under the overhang.
  • The gap between disc and belt is adjustable and is set smaller at each successive disc, so the field rises along the belt.

Functioning.

  1. The feed passes under the first disc, where the gap is largest. Only strongly magnetic particles jump to the rim.
  2. The rotating disc carries them beyond the belt edge, where the field falls away, and they drop into the first side chute.
  3. Under the second and third discs the field is stronger, so progressively weaker magnetic particles are lifted and dropped into their own chutes.
  4. Non-magnetic particles stay on the belt and leave over its end as tailings.

Control and use. Gap, magnet current, belt speed and feed rate set the cuts. The feed must be dry and closely sized. Typical uses: separating ilmenite, garnet and monazite (weakly magnetic) from zircon and rutile in beach sands, and wolframite from cassiterite.
pts: Neat labelled sketch: belt, magnet poles below, rotating discs above with decreasing gaps, side chutes, non-magnetic discharge

Force depends on the field gradient (F \propto \chi V B\,dB/dx); the sharp disc rim concentrates the field
Construction: dry feed in a thin layer on a belt passing between magnet poles below and rotating discs above
Magnetic particles are lifted to the disc rim, carried beyond the belt edge where the field falls, and dropped into a side chute
Successive discs with smaller gaps (stronger field) take off progressively weaker magnetic fractions
Non-magnetic particles stay on the belt and discharge over its end
An application (beach sands: ilmenite or monazite from zircon and rutile; wolframite from cassiterite) or the control variables (gap, current, belt speed, feed rate)

4b.html:
Collectors are organic reagents that adsorb on the selected mineral and make its surface hydrophobic, so that it attaches to air bubbles and floats.

They are heteropolar: a polar group reacts with the mineral surface and a non-polar hydrocarbon chain faces the water, so the surface seen by the water is hydrocarbon. Example: sodium ethyl xanthate, \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2Na} (100-750 g/t), dissociates and the -\mathrm{S^-} of \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2^-} bonds to \mathrm{Pb^{2+}} at a galena surface.

Types: anionic (xanthates, dithiophosphates), cationic (amines), and non-ionising oils.
pts: Defines collectors as reagents that adsorb on the chosen mineral and make it hydrophobic so it attaches to bubbles
Heteropolar structure: polar group on the mineral, non-polar hydrocarbon chain facing the water
Example: xanthate, whose -\mathrm{S^-} bonds to sulphide surface cations
Types: anionic and cationic (or ionising and non-ionising)

4c.html:
The process. Air bubbles are passed through a pulp of fine mineral particles in water. Particles that water does not wet (hydrophobic) attach to the bubbles, rise and form a froth on the surface, which is skimmed off as the concentrate. Wetted (hydrophilic) particles stay in the pulp and leave as tailings.

Driving force. Attachment replaces a solid-liquid and a liquid-gas interface by a new solid-gas interface. It is stable only if the surface energy of the system falls. Per unit area:

\Delta G = \gamma_{sg} - (\gamma_{sl} + \gamma_{lg}) < 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \gamma_{sg} - \gamma_{sl} < \gamma_{lg}

With Young's equation at the three-phase contact, \gamma_{sg} = \gamma_{sl} + \gamma_{lg}\cos\theta, where \theta is the contact angle measured through the water:

\Delta G = \gamma_{lg}(\cos\theta - 1)

So a mineral with a larger contact angle attaches more strongly; when \theta \approx 0 the mineral is fully wetted and \Delta G \approx 0.

Why minerals differ. Breaking ionic or covalent bonds leaves charged surface sites that attract polar water molecules, so most minerals are hydrophilic. Solids held by van der Waals forces (sulphur, graphite, talc, molybdenite) leave uncharged surfaces and are naturally hydrophobic. Hence collectors are adsorbed to make the chosen mineral hydrophobic, and a frother keeps the bubbles and froth stable.

Limits. Only fairly fine particles float: if a particle is too large, its weight (and the fluid motion) exceeds the bubble-particle adhesion and the bubble drops its load.

Direct and reverse flotation. Normally the value mineral goes to the froth and the gangue stays in the pulp (direct flotation); in reverse flotation the gangue is floated.
pts: Describes the process: bubbles through a pulp, hydrophobic particles attach and rise into a froth that is skimmed; hydrophilic particles stay in the pulp
Driving force is the reduction of surface energy: a solid-gas interface replaces solid-liquid and liquid-gas, so attachment needs \gamma_{sg} - \gamma_{sl} < \gamma_{lg}
Contact angle with Young's equation, \Delta G = \gamma_{lg}(\cos\theta - 1), larger \theta means more hydrophobic
Links wettability to bonding: broken ionic or covalent bonds give charged, hydrophilic surfaces; van der Waals-bonded solids (the course book adds hydrogen-bonded ones) are hydrophobic
States that collectors impart hydrophobicity to the chosen mineral and a frother stabilises the froth
Only fine particles float, because a large particle's weight exceeds the adhesion to the bubble
Distinguishes direct flotation (mineral floated) from reverse flotation (gangue floated)

  • Being hydrophobic is necessary but not sufficient: fluid motion and particle mass also act against attachment, which is why the size range is limited.
  • The course book also calls hydrogen-bonded solids hydrophobic; that is doubtful, because a surface with broken hydrogen bonds hydrogen-bonds to water (ice and gypsum wet readily). The naturally floatable minerals are van der Waals solids such as graphite, sulphur, talc and molybdenite.

5a.html:
Smelting and matte smelting

Smelting (reduction smelting) heats an ore, usually an oxide, with a flux and a reducing agent (coke) so that the oxide is reduced and the charge melts into liquid metal and an immiscible slag, with gases leaving:

\text{mineral} + \text{gangue} + \text{flux} + \text{reducing agent} \rightarrow \text{metal} + \text{slag} + \text{gas}, \qquad \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}

Matte smelting fuses a sulphide concentrate (usually partly roasted) with a flux, without a reducing agent, to give a matte, a molten mixture of sulphides (\mathrm{Cu_2S} and FeS), under an immiscible slag; some sulphur leaves as \mathrm{SO_2}.

BasisSmeltingMatte smelting
Chargeoxide ore, flux, cokesulphide concentrate or calcine, siliceous flux
Chemistryreduction by C and COmainly melting; Fe partly oxidised and slagged
Atmospherereducingneutral to mildly oxidising
Productcrude metal (iron, lead)matte, an intermediate that must be converted
GasCO, \mathrm{CO_2}\mathrm{SO_2}

Extraction of copper by matte smelting

The process works because copper has a greater affinity for sulphur, and iron a greater affinity for oxygen: iron is oxidised and slagged, and copper stays as \mathrm{Cu_2S}.

  1. Concentration. Chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}) ore with less than 2% Cu is upgraded by froth flotation to a concentrate of about 11 to 35% Cu.
  2. Partial roasting. Part of the FeS is oxidised; the reaction is not completed, so that no higher iron oxides form:
2\,\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
  1. Matte smelting. The calcine is melted with quartz at 1200 to 1300 °C (reverberatory or flash furnace). Any copper oxide is turned back to sulphide, and FeO is slagged:
\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

The denser matte collects below the slag; the slag is tapped off and discarded.

  1. Converting. Air is blown through the molten matte. Slag blow: FeS is oxidised and slagged, and the slag is poured off, leaving white metal (\mathrm{Cu_2S}):
2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

Copper blow:

2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}

The product is blister copper, about 99% Cu.

  1. Refining. Fire refining blows air to remove the dissolved sulphur ([\mathrm{S}] + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{SO_2}), then removes the dissolved oxygen with hydrocarbons (poling), for example \mathrm{CH_4} + 3\,[\mathrm{O}] = \mathrm{CO} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}; S falls from about 0.02 to 0.002% and O from 0.5 to 0.05%. The anodes are electrorefined to cathode copper of 99.99% Cu.
pts: Smelting: ore, flux and a reducing agent (coke) heated to give liquid metal, slag and gas, with a reduction such as \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}
Matte smelting: sulphide charge fused with flux, no reducing agent, gives a matte (molten \mathrm{Cu_2S} + FeS) and an immiscible slag
At least two contrasts: metal against an intermediate that needs converting, reducing against neutral or oxidising conditions, oxide against sulphide feed, CO against \mathrm{SO_2}
Principle: Cu has the greater affinity for S and Fe for O, so Fe goes to slag and Cu to matte (or gives the sequence concentration, roasting, smelting, converting, refining)
Concentration of chalcopyrite (below 2% Cu) by froth flotation to about 11 to 35% Cu

Partial roasting with balanced reactions (2\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}; 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2}), not taken to completion

Matte smelting with silica at 1200 to 1300 °C: \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}, and \mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO} or "very little reaction, mainly melting"
Matte and slag immiscible; the denser matte settles below and the slag is removed
Converting, slag blow: 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and slagging with \mathrm{SiO_2}; slag poured off
Converting, copper blow: 2\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}, giving blister copper of about 99% Cu
Refining: fire refining (S oxidised by air, O removed by hydrocarbons or poling) and electrorefining to about 99.99% Cu

  • Do not write that carbon reduces the matte: matte smelting needs no reducing agent, and copper is made from \mathrm{Cu_2S} by the reaction of \mathrm{Cu_2O} with \mathrm{Cu_2S} in the converter.
  • The roast is stopped short because \mathrm{Fe_3O_4} and \mathrm{Fe_2O_3} melt high and are hard to slag; magnetite makes the slag viscous and traps matte.

5b.html:
Zone refining is a method of purifying a fairly pure metal. A narrow molten zone is moved slowly along a partly purified solid bar. Impurities that lower the melting point collect in the liquid, travel with the zone to the far end, and that end is cut off.

From the phase diagram. The liquidus and the solidus both fall from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus more steeply, so at every temperature the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium with it:

k = \frac{C_S}{C_L} < 1

A melt of composition X (C_0) starts to freeze at L_1 and deposits solid S_1 with only kC_0.

Effect of the moving zone. Purer solid freezes at the back of the zone; the rejected impurity stays in the zone, which melts fresh charge at its front, so the impurity is carried forward. The first solid holds kC_0, and the last zone length freezes impure and is cropped.

Multiple passes in the same direction: the more passes, the purer the starting end. For k = 0.3 the start holds 0.3C_0 after one pass and about 0.01C_0 after five.

Conditions. k far from 1 and slow zone travel. Impurities with k > 1 move the other way, to the starting end. The method gives ultra-pure Si, Ge and Ga.
pts: Defines zone refining: a narrow molten zone moved slowly along a solid bar sweeps the impurities into the liquid and to one end, which is cut off
Phase diagram: temperature against impurity concentration, liquidus and solidus falling from T_m of the pure metal, three fields labelled, tie lines S_1L_1 and S_2L_2
States from the diagram that the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium, k = C_S/C_L < 1 (S_1 purer than L_1)
The purer solid freezes at the back of the zone and the rejected impurity is carried forward; the first solid holds kC_0 and the impure last part is cropped
Multiple passes in the same direction raise the purity at the starting end
A condition or use: k far from 1, slow zone travel, impurities with k > 1 move to the starting end, or products such as Si, Ge, Ga
5b.sketch:
• Axes: temperature (vertical) against impurity (solute) concentration (horizontal).
  • Liquidus and solidus both falling from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus below and steeper.
  • Fields labelled Liquid, Solid + Liquid, Solid.
  • Vertical line X for the melt C_0; tie line S_1 L_1 where freezing starts and S_2 L_2 where it ends.
  • k = C_S/C_L < 1 written on the diagram.
5b.watch:
• The phase diagram carries the marks for "principles": label the axes, both lines and the tie line, and say which composition is the solid.
  • Do not say the impurity "evaporates" or is "removed" in the zone: it is only redistributed along the bar, and the impure end must be cut off.
  • Fast zone travel lets the rejected impurity build up ahead of the freezing front, so the effective k moves towards 1 and each pass removes much less impurity.
  • Extra depth: silicon is refined by the floating-zone method (no container) because molten Si reacts with crucible materials and picks up oxygen and other contamination; after many passes the profile reaches a limiting (ultimate) distribution, set by k and the zone length.

5c.html:
Definition. A predominance area (Kellogg) diagram is an isothermal plot, drawn from thermodynamic data, of \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} for a metal-sulphur-oxygen system. It shows the area in which each condensed phase (metal, sulphide, oxide, sulphate) is stable. Each line is a two-phase equilibrium, for example

\mathrm{NiS} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{NiO} + \mathrm{SO_2}: \quad \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} = \log K + \tfrac{3}{2}\log p_{\mathrm{O_2}}

Uses.

  1. Shows which product a given roaster gas and temperature give, so conditions can be set for an oxide (dead roast), a sulphate (for leaching) or a partial roast.
  2. Superimposed diagrams of two metals (Cu and Fe) show conditions for selective sulphation.

Limitations.

  1. Equilibrium only: no rates, so real products may differ.
  2. Pure condensed phases at unit activity assumed (no solid solutions, mattes, ferrites).
  3. Valid for one temperature only.
pts: Defines it as an isothermal \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} diagram showing the stable condensed phase in each area
Lines from equilibrium constants of the phase reactions, with an example
Use: setting roasting conditions for the desired product (oxide, sulphate, partial roast)
Use: selective roasting of two metals by superimposed diagrams
Two limitations from: equilibrium only (no kinetics), pure phases at unit activity, one temperature only
5c.watch:
• Name the axes and say "at constant temperature"; that is the definition.
  • A sulphating roast is favoured by low temperature and high \mathrm{SO_2} and \mathrm{O_2} (upper right of the diagram); a dead roast to oxide needs a higher temperature or a leaner gas.

6a.html:
Essential features

A successful hydrometallurgical process must carry out four steps well:

  1. Leaching. The desired constituent (usually the value mineral, sometimes the gangue) must dissolve selectively and fast enough in a cheap leaching reagent. Ore preparation (grinding, sizing, beneficiation, roasting) is added where needed.
  2. Separation of the leach liquor from the solid residue by settling, thickening, filtration and washing.
  3. Recovery of the metal values from the liquor (after purification) by precipitation, cementation, electrolysis, ion exchange, solvent extraction or evaporation.
  4. Recovery of the reagent. The leachant is purified, readjusted and recycled; for example, the \mathrm{H_2SO_4} used in leaching is regenerated in electrowinning.

When it is preferred to pyrometallurgy

  • Lean and complex ores. Smelting would heat and slag all the gangue, but leaching is selective (siliceous gangue is unattacked), so reagent cost follows the metal content. Gold ore with about 10 g/t (10 ppm) is cyanided economically, while smelting it is out of the question.
  • Sulphide ores where \mathrm{SO_2} is a problem: leaching keeps the sulphur in solution, so pollution is less.
  • Recovery of by-products and pure products: each step can be controlled closely.
  • Small start: a plant can start small and expand, while a smelter must be large.
  • Costly coke, mild temperatures and mild corrosion (no refractory relining shutdowns).

For high-grade ores and concentrates, however, pyrometallurgy usually needs less energy per tonne of metal (concentrated streams, fast reactions, exothermic reactions), so it is normally chosen there.
pts: Leaching: selective dissolution of the wanted constituent (value or gangue) in a suitable, cheap reagent at an adequate rate, with ore preparation as needed
Separation of the leach liquor from the residue (settling, thickening, filtration, washing)
Recovery of metal values from the liquor (precipitation, cementation, electrolysis, ion exchange, solvent extraction)
Reagent recovery and recycling, for example acid regenerated in electrowinning
Preferred for lean and complex ores because leaching is selective and the gangue need not be slagged (gold at about 10 g/t by cyanidation)
Preferred for sulphides where \mathrm{SO_2} pollution must be avoided
Any two further conditions: by-product recovery and close control, small-scale start, costly coke, mild temperature and corrosion
States that for high-grade ores pyrometallurgy usually needs less energy (concentrated streams, fast and exothermic reactions)

• "Essential features" is read here as the four steps and what each must achieve; a student who lists the advantages of hydrometallurgy under this heading should still get the condition marks below.
  • Do not claim that hydrometallurgy always saves energy: at room temperature it burns no fuel, but for rich ores pyrometallurgy needs less energy per tonne.

6b.html:
Common types of leaching reagent

  1. Water: dissolves soluble salts such as \mathrm{CuSO_4} and \mathrm{ZnSO_4}; some low-grade copper sulphides slowly weather to soluble sulphate. Plain water is rarely used commercially.
  2. Acids: mineral acids, above all \mathrm{H_2SO_4}, are the most common. Their strong action often makes fine grinding unnecessary, and the acid consumed in leaching is regenerated during electrolysis.
  3. Bases: hot concentrated NaOH under pressure leaches bauxite; \mathrm{NH_4OH} leaches native copper, copper ores, NiS and \mathrm{Cu_2S}.
  4. Aqueous salt solutions: NaCN dissolves gold:
4\mathrm{Au} + 8\mathrm{NaCN} + \mathrm{O_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NaAu(CN)_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH}

Secondary oxidising or reducing reagents aid dissolution, for example \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} for CuS and \mathrm{SO_2} for \mathrm{MnO_2}.

Criteria for an effective reagent

  • Selectivity for the desired constituent; it depends on the reagent concentration, temperature and contact time.
  • Cost: cheap. Selectivity and cost are the most important factors.
  • Rapid leaching: soluble enough to make a strong solution, which leaches fast and keeps volumes small.
  • Low corrosion of the materials of construction (chlorides are severe), and non-toxic to plant personnel.
  • Regeneration: it should be recoverable and recycled.
  • Suited to the chemical and physical character of the material being leached.
pts: Water: soluble sulphates such as \mathrm{CuSO_4}, \mathrm{ZnSO_4}; rarely used on its own
Acids: \mathrm{H_2SO_4} the most common, strong enough to avoid fine grinding, regenerated in electrolysis
Bases: hot concentrated NaOH under pressure for bauxite; \mathrm{NH_4OH} for native Cu, Cu ores, NiS, \mathrm{Cu_2S}
Salt solutions: NaCN for gold, with the balanced cyanidation equation
Oxidising or reducing aids such as \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} or \mathrm{SO_2}
Selectivity (set by concentration, temperature, contact time) and cost, named as the most important criteria
Fast leaching from a sufficiently strong solution
Low corrosion of plant materials and low toxicity
Regenerable, and suited to the character of the ore

  • The cyanide equation is a frequent loss of marks: count Na, O and H on both sides.

6c.html:
A potential/pH (Pourbaix) diagram shows the predominant species of a metal at equilibrium at each reduction potential E and pH, for a chosen ion activity (10^{-3} for leaching), with the two water stability lines drawn on it.

Importance in leaching.

  1. Choice of conditions. It shows whether the mineral can dissolve at all and over what pH and E its ion stays in solution. The pH is then set with acid or alkali and E with an oxidant, reductant or applied potential.
  2. Zinc example. Zn and ZnO dissolve as \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9 and as \mathrm{ZnO_2^{2-}} above about 13.4; leaching is more efficient farther from the boundary.
  3. Need for an oxidant. Zn (-0.76 V) lies below both water lines and dissolves in acid with \mathrm{H_2} evolution; Cu (+0.34 V) lies between them and needs \mathrm{O_2} or \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}; Au (+1.50 V) lies above both and needs cyanide to complex it.

So the diagram fixes the reagent, pH and oxidant; the rate must still be found by experiment.
pts: Shows the predominant species at each E and pH as domains for a chosen ion activity, with the water lines drawn on
Used to choose the leaching pH (acid or alkali) and potential (oxidant, reductant or applied potential)
Zn example: \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9 or zincate above about 13.4
Water-line comparison: Zn dissolves with \mathrm{H_2} evolution, Cu needs \mathrm{O_2} or another oxidant, Au needs a complexing agent such as cyanide
Notes that the diagram gives feasibility, not rate

7a.html:
The two situations (sketches)

In both, the reagent R must reach the mineral surface and the dissolved metal species M and other products P must move away, across a liquid boundary layer at the surface.

(a) The mineral dissolves completely. No solid product forms and the surface recedes, for example CuO in dilute \mathrm{H_2SO_4}. R falls from [R]_B in the bulk to [R]_S at the surface; M and P fall from [M]_S, [P]_S to [M]_B, [P]_B.

(b) The mineral decomposes and dissolves only in part. A solid residue forms, for example \mathrm{CaWO_4 + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow CaCO_3 + WO_4^{2-}}. Leaching continues only if the residue is porous. I is the mineral/residue and II the residue/solution interface.

Kinetic steps

Case (a): (1) diffusion of R from the bulk to the mineral-solution interface; (2) reaction at the interface to a soluble metal species; (3) diffusion of M and P away into the bulk.

Case (b), the general case: (1) diffusion of R from the bulk to interface II; (2) diffusion of R through the porous product layer; (3) reaction with the mineral at interface I; (4) outward diffusion of M and P through the layer; (5) diffusion of M and P from II into the bulk. Without a residue, steps 2 and 4 vanish. The slowest step sets the rate, so it must be known before a remedy is chosen.

Accelerating the leaching

  • Film diffusion (steps 1, 5) controlling: stir or agitate. The boundary layer thins, so the rate rises with stirring speed until the layer reaches a limiting thickness; high-speed propellers or turbines are used.
  • Reaction (step 3) controlling: agitation has no effect. Raise the temperature (activation energy 10-25 kcal/mol, 42-105 kJ/mol), the reagent concentration (according to the reaction order) or the oxidant pressure.
  • Pore diffusion (steps 2, 4): stirring does not reach inside the layer; finer grinding shortens the path.
  • In every case: finer grinding exposes more surface, and higher temperature speeds up all steps; diffusion (5 kcal/mol or less) gains least.
pts: Sketch (a): mineral and solution with [R] falling from [R]_B to [R]_S and [M], [P] falling from surface to bulk values, labelled
Sketch (b): porous residue with interfaces I and II and the R, M, P profiles labelled with subscripts I and II
Explains situation (a): complete dissolution with no solid product, with an example (CuO in dilute acid)
Explains situation (b): partial dissolution leaving a residue that must be porous for leaching to continue, with an example (\mathrm{CaWO_4} in carbonate)
Case (a) three steps: reagent diffusion to the surface, surface reaction, product diffusion away
Case (b) five steps, including diffusion of R through the porous layer, reaction at interface I and outward diffusion of M and P through the layer
Film diffusion control: stirring or agitation thins the boundary layer, rate rising to a plateau
Reaction control: agitation has no effect; raise temperature (activation energy 10-25 kcal/mol, 42-105 kJ/mol), reagent concentration or oxidant pressure
Finer grinding raises the surface area and shortens the pore path, which stirring cannot help
Higher temperature speeds up every step, diffusion least (5 kcal/mol or less)

7b.html:
Why purify

Leaching is rarely completely selective, so the pregnant liquor carries ions that interfere with later steps or contaminate the product. Purification removes them, or removes the desired metal selectively and leaves them behind (selective precipitation, ion exchange, solvent extraction).

Principle

Metal ions in solution exchange with specific ions held by a solid resin or a second liquid phase; the exchange is reversible and stoichiometric, so it removes unwanted ions or concentrates a selected one. The resin is an insoluble, chemically stable 3-D polymer framework of porous beads (0.5-1 mm); functional groups bonded to it supply the exchangeable ions and control the selectivity.

\begin{aligned} \text{cation exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{2\,R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}\\ \text{anion exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{R^+Cl^- + A^- \rightleftharpoons R^+A^- + Cl^-} \end{aligned}

The cycle

  1. Loading: clear liquor flows through columns of resin, which takes up the metal ion; the barren solution is dumped.
  2. Elution: a small volume of strong solution reverses the reaction, giving a concentrated, pure eluate.
  3. Regeneration of the resin for the next cycle.

Example: uranium

\mathrm{H_2SO_4} leaching gives the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, while impurity metals are cations, so an anion resin takes only the uranium:

\begin{aligned} \text{loading:}&\quad \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-} + 2R_2SO_4 \rightarrow R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 2SO_4^{2-}}\\ \text{elution (acidified chloride):}&\quad \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl^- \rightarrow 4RCl + [UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}\\ \text{regeneration:}&\quad \mathrm{4RCl + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2R_2SO_4 + 4HCl} \end{aligned}

Plant and result

Columns A and B load in series while C is eluted; when A is saturated the columns change over, so the contact is counter-current. Impurities stay in the barren solution (purification); since both steps are nearly 100 % efficient, the metal is concentrated by about V_{\text{liquor}}/V_{\text{eluate}} (concentration).
pts: Need for purification: leaching is not selective, impurities interfere or contaminate; ion exchange is one of the methods
Principle: ions in solution exchange with ions on a solid resin (or a second liquid); reversible and stoichiometric
Resin: insoluble, stable 3-D polymer framework as porous beads; bonded functional groups supply the exchangeable ions and control selectivity
A general exchange reaction for a cation or an anion exchanger

8a.html:
An electrolyte for metal extraction or refining should:

  1. High ionic conductivity, so the IR drop and energy are low.
  2. High solubility of the metal salt, giving a high metal-ion concentration (cryolite dissolves \mathrm{Al_2O_3}).
  3. Stability: only the wanted metal is discharged; other constituents have higher decomposition voltages and do not volatilise or hydrolyse.
  4. No attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell lining; a dense, adherent deposit.
  5. Cheap, easily purified and regenerated. A fused-salt bath also needs a low melting point and a density different from the metal.
pts: High electrical (ionic) conductivity, to keep the voltage and energy low
High solubility of the metal compound, giving an adequate metal-ion concentration
Chemical and electrochemical stability: no constituent other than the metal is discharged, no volatilisation or hydrolysis
No chemical attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell materials (a sound deposit results)
Cheap, easily purified and regenerated, or (fused salt) low melting point and a density different from the metal

8b.html:
Relative activity. The electrochemical series ranks metals by their standard reduction potential against the hydrogen electrode (0 V). The more negative E^\circ, the more reactive the metal and the harder its ion is to reduce: Au +1.50, Ag +0.80, Cu +0.34, H 0.00, Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76, Mn -1.18, Al -1.66, Mg -2.37, Na -2.71 V.

Cathode competition. In water the metal ion competes with hydrogen, and the reaction with the more positive deposition potential wins:

E_{\mathrm{M}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}} + \frac{0.0592}{z}\log a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}} - \eta_{\mathrm{M}}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}} = -0.0592\,\mathrm{pH} - \eta_{\mathrm{H}}

The metal deposits when E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}}; \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is the hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode surface.

1. Metals nobler than hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au). E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}} even in strong acid and at low metal activity, so they deposit readily. Hydrogen appears mainly when the current density approaches the limiting current. Copper is won from about 150-180 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 85-95 % current efficiency.

2. Less noble metals with a high hydrogen overvoltage (Zn, Cd, Pb, Sn, Mn). By equilibrium hydrogen should evolve first, but on these metals \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is about 0.7-1 V (against below 0.1 V on Pt), which pushes E_{\mathrm{H}} below E_{\mathrm{M}}. Zinc is won at 400-600 A/m^2, 35-40 ^\circC, on Al cathodes, at about 90 % efficiency, but only from a deeply purified electrolyte: Co, Ni, Sb, Ge lower \eta_{\mathrm{H}} and re-dissolve the zinc.

3. Less noble metals with a low hydrogen overvoltage (Fe, Ni, Co). They need a weakly acid (pH about 2-4), warm electrolyte and give lower efficiency.

4. Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na, Ca, Li, Ti). E^\circ lies below about -1.6 V: no attainable overvoltage stops hydrogen evolution, the current goes to \mathrm{H_2}, and any metal formed reacts with water:

\mathrm{2Al + 6H_2O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_2}

Conclusion. Whether a metal can be electrowon from water is set by its potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration. The most reactive metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis: Al from cryolite-alumina, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl.
pts: Explains the electrochemical series: metals ranked by E^\circ against hydrogen (0 V), more negative means more reactive, with values
At the cathode the reaction with the more positive deposition potential occurs first; metal ion and \mathrm{H^+} compete (Nernst forms for both)
Nobler metals (Cu, Ag, Au) deposit readily even from strong acid; hydrogen mainly near the limiting current
Less noble metals: thermodynamically hydrogen should be discharged first
Hydrogen overvoltage (high on Zn, Pb, Hg; low on Pt) moves the hydrogen potential below that of the metal, so Zn, Cd, Pb, Mn can deposit
Operating conditions for zinc (high current density, low temperature, pure electrolyte free of Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) and about 90 % efficiency
Fe, Ni, Co with low overvoltage need pH control and give lower efficiency
Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na; E^\circ below about -1.6 V): hydrogen evolves instead and the metal would react with water (balanced equation)
Concludes that such metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis, with examples (Hall-Heroult Al, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl)
States the overall criterion: potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration

8c.html:
Aluminium (E^\circ = -1.66 V) cannot be deposited from water, so it is won by fused-salt electrolysis of alumina dissolved in cryolite (Hall-Heroult process, 1886).

Raw material. Bauxite is purified by the Bayer process (NaOH digestion, red mud rejected, \mathrm{Al(OH)_3} precipitated and calcined) to pure \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, since oxides less stable than alumina (\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}, \mathrm{SiO_2}) would be reduced into the metal.

Electrolyte. Molten cryolite, \mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}, with about 2-6 % \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, excess \mathrm{AlF_3} and about 5 % \mathrm{CaF_2}, at about 950-970 ^\circC. Cryolite dissolves alumina (m.p. 2050 ^\circC) at a much lower temperature, conducts well, and its density (about 2.1 g/cm^3) is below that of liquid Al (about 2.3 g/cm^3), so the metal collects under the bath, protected from air.

Cell. A steel shell lined with insulation and carbon blocks (cathode, with steel collector bars); a pool of molten Al is the working cathode surface. Carbon anodes (prebaked or Soderberg) dip into the bath about 4-5 cm above the metal. A frozen crust covered with alumina insulates the top and frozen bath protects the side walls.

Reactions.

\text{cathode: } \mathrm{Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al(l)} \qquad \text{anode: } \mathrm{2O^{2-} + C \rightarrow CO_2 + 4e^-}
\text{overall: } \mathrm{2Al_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Al + 3CO_2}

The anode burns away (theory 0.33, practice about 0.4-0.45 kg C per kg Al), which lowers the reversible voltage from about 2.2 V to about 1.2 V.

Operation. About 4-4.5 V per cell, 150-500 kA, current efficiency 90-96 %, energy about 12.5-15 kWh per kg Al. Alumina is fed through the crust by point feeders. If it falls below about 2 %, the anode effect occurs: the voltage jumps to 20-50 V and \mathrm{CF_4} forms. Aluminium (about 99.7 %) is siphoned off daily and cast; off-gas fluorides are caught on alumina in dry scrubbers and returned.

Assessment. The process is simple and continuous, but energy-intensive, and the anodes release about 1.5 kg \mathrm{CO_2} per kg Al. Hence the work on inert anodes and on lower cell voltages.
pts: Reason for fused salt: Al (-1.66 V) cannot be deposited from aqueous solution
Feed: pure alumina from bauxite by the Bayer process (NaOH digestion, red mud out, calcination)
Role of cryolite: dissolves alumina at about 950-970 ^\circC (alumina melts at 2050 ^\circC), conducts, and is lighter than liquid Al so the metal sinks
Bath composition: about 2-6 % \mathrm{Al_2O_3} with \mathrm{AlF_3} and \mathrm{CaF_2} additions
Cell construction: carbon-lined steel shell as cathode with collector bars, molten Al pad, consumable carbon anodes (prebaked or Soderberg), frozen crust and side ledge
Electrode reactions and the balanced overall reaction \mathrm{2Al_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Al + 3CO_2}, with anode consumption
Operating data: about 4-4.5 V, current efficiency about 90-96 %, energy about 12.5-15 kWh/kg Al
Alumina feeding through the crust and the anode effect at low alumina
Tapping of about 99.7 % Al, fluoride capture in dry scrubbers, and an assessment (high energy use, \mathrm{CO_2} from the anodes)
